The *Mokṣakārikā* composed by the teacher Sadyojyotiḥśiva,
together with the commentary composed by Bhaṭṭa Rāmakaṇṭha.
Sadyojyotis and Bṛhaspati, by whom the path was illuminated through their perfected state within the Siddhānta— those two are to be revered even by the gurus.
Having bowed to Śaṅkara, the bestower of both worldly enjoyment and liberation, for the sake of enjoyment and liberation,
I shall briefly explain the *Mokṣakārikā* concerning enjoyment and liberation.

For here, having first made the formal proposition: "I shall explain both enjoyment and liberation, along with their means, as established in the *Ruru-siddhānta*" (*Bhoga-kārikā* 2), [the author] stated: "The enjoyment of the enjoyer is the manifestation of consciousness" (*Bhoga-kārikā* 73), and so forth. Thus, enjoyment and the enjoyers—the bound souls (*paśu*) who are devoid of autonomy—and the means of their enjoyment, consisting of the body, organs, and so on, from the element earth up to *kalā*, have been described.
The universe and its material cause, which is Māyā, have already been established; now, however, for the sake of accomplishing experience,
another means— the definition of the agent— is stated to address whether that [universe] proceeds by itself or is impelled by an agent.

Unconnected with birth and impurity, omniscient, the creator of all, and all-pervading; possessing both parts and being partless, infinite, He performs His endless effects according to His own will. (1)
Having manifested His unsurpassed sovereignty by agitating Māyā through His powers,
Śiva creates the manifold universe for the enjoyment of those who experience worldly existence.
The universe, previously described as having *māyā* as its material cause (*upādāna*), consists of the means of experience and has *adṛṣṭa* (unseen merit/demerit) as its agent.

Since it is a specific effect, its being produced by an agent possessing specific knowledge and action is certain, just like [the production of] a jar by a potter and so forth. Thus, because the universe possesses parts (*sāvayavatva*), the reason is not unestablished (*asiddha*); nor is it inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), for this applies even to everything that has *adṛṣṭa* as its agent, such as forests, flowers, and the like.

Because it has been made the subject (*pakṣīkṛtatvāt*). For this very reason, it is not contradictory (*viruddha*), because there is no pervasion (*vyāpti*) with the opposite. Furthermore, it has been stated elsewhere that the definition of a logical reason (*hetu-lakṣaṇa*) cannot be established through the three criteria (*trairūpya*). [Objection: But surely, since the pervasion is established in the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) together with an ignorant agent, this reason leads to the possibility that the creator of the universe is indeed ignorant; thus, there is a contradiction with what is intended (*iṣṭa-vyāghāta*)? [Response: No.

By this, even that [potter] is indeed one whose connection with impurity has not arisen; for even the potter, in the accomplishment of his own work, lacks a connection with impurity—that is, ignorance. For if ignorance or delusion were present there, he would not produce a jar at all;
rather, the potter would produce bricks or a pot and the like with defective parts, which would be useless for the purpose.

For example, just as upon seeing a pot with all its parts complete, a potter endowed with excellence of intellect is inferred— and not one who is ignorant or deluded— so too, when God is inferred from His own effect characterized as the universe, He is inferred as being entirely free from the connection with impurity; thus, there is no subversion of our desired conclusion.

But surely, a potter indeed possesses ignorance regarding things other than his own work? Let it be so; the point of the analogy is that he lacks such ignorance regarding the specific subject at hand, namely the pot. But does this not lead to the undesirable consequence that the Lord likewise possesses ignorance regarding things other than His own work? No, for [He lacks it] regarding His own effects, which are the means for the experience of enjoyment and liberation.
Because there is no other entity apart from the universe.
Now, one might ask: "How do you know that there is nothing else? Let it be so; if that [other] were a means for experience, then, like the body and its organs, it would simply be an effect.
But if it is not a means for that [experience], then since it would serve no purpose, ignorance regarding it—just as in the case of a rabbit's horn—is merely an ornament.

Regarding this, they say: "He who is the knower of the reality of what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted, along with their means of attainment, is accepted as a valid authority (*pramāṇa*), but not one who knows everything. For this very reason, since there is nothing else apart from the universe, he is omniscient and the maker of all; thus the Creator of the Universe is established as both the knower of his own effects and the maker of all things, even in the case of a potter, for it is established that he possesses knowledge and agency regarding his own work. Indeed, it is not [otherwise] for him...

In this regard, it has been stated that if there were even a partial lack of knowledge or a deficiency in power, the jar would not come into being from that [cause]. For this very reason, [the Lord] is all-pervasive (*vibhu*) because He pervades His own effects, just like a potter; for if the potter did not pervade his own effects—the broad base, the belly, and the rim—his status as the agent would not be established with respect to them, just as it is not established with respect to mountains and the like.

Is it not the case that a body is also obtained for the creator of the universe, just as it is for the existence of an effect? No; for even in the case of potters and others, their own bodily movements and other effects are not observed to be preceded by another body. Is it not true that even those [movements] are produced solely by will?
True; therefore, the entire collection of effects does not deviate from him alone as its cause.
There is no fault in this, for even the Creator of the Universe is inferred to perform His work immediately following His will. Now, one might object: "Will is a modification of the mind;
how can it be possible for the Creator of the Universe? We reply: Will is not a modification of the mind even for beings like us;

rather, as we have stated in our *Mantravārttika-ṭīkā*, it is simply the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*), which—like the power of knowledge—is manifested by the intellect (*buddhi*) and made manifest by the mind (*manas*).

"For indeed, the will of that mind which possesses power (śākta) is itself the power of action (kriyā-śakti). Therefore, because the Lord's power is unobstructed, there is no need for a manifesting agent. Now, it may be argued: "It is observed that the will acts as the agent of the movement and so forth of a body presided over by it, even without dependence on another body; however, this would not apply to external objects such as a jar produced from clay and the like. True.

For this very reason, the universe is always inferred to be his body, as it were, because it is that which is to be presided over by him. And for this same reason, based on the observation of effects, one infers only the totality of his powers of knowledge, action, and will, and not a connection with a body composed of *kalā*, *rāga*, *vidyā*, and so forth,
because such a connection would involve logical fallacy (*vyabhicāra*).

"He shall be both with parts (*sakala*) and without parts (*niṣkala*), the creator of the universe," as will be stated hereafter. Furthermore, He is infinite because of His possession of powers such as omniscience, just like the Self (*ātman*). The infinity and omnipresence of selves have already been established in the section on experience (*bhoga-prakaraṇa*); therefore, He too is all-pervading (*vibhu*). Now, one might object: "The multiplicity of effects, such as pots and cloths, is established as being invariably concomitant with a multiplicity of agents; [is this not the case] here too for the elements from earth down to water? [To this we reply:]...

There are many things denoted by the word "universe," for indeed, on the grounds of being effects, many creators of the universe could be inferred? True; this would be the case if these [effects] did not have a single purpose consisting of experience. And that they do have such a purpose has been established in passages such as: "Consciousness, intensified by *kalā*, has the sphere of objects shown by *vidyā*... (Svāyambhuvasūtrasaṃgraha 3.10). Furthermore, whatever is diverse yet serves a single purpose is produced by a single intelligent creator, as in the case of a palace and the like.

"Certainty" means possessing unsurpassed sovereignty, because He alone is the creator of the entire universe; and that Śiva, being engaged solely for the sake of benefiting others, is endowed with those attributes everywhere and is established by valid means of knowledge. || 1-2 ||
Regarding this, another [opponent] speaks in the shadow of the Sāṃkhya system:
"A variegated cloth is seen to arise from a variegated thread, not from Śiva;
just so, the world is variegated because it arises from a variegated seed, not from Śiva. (3)
It is not appropriate to say this while denying the weaver who provides assistance to the cloth, for that would involve further contradiction.
Rather, even though he exists, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of this reason in the example by Śiva, the creator of the universe, is unestablished; thus, there is inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatā*).
It is precisely the power of illusion (*māyā*) belonging to the creator of the world that serves as the probans. For an effect does not deviate from its material cause.
This is not a fault:
apart from the intellect and activity of the weaver, no insentient material cause designated as "threads" is observed to be the cause of the cloth. (4)
Just as that [earth], so too the insentient primordial matter (*upādāna*) is the seed of the world;
apart from the knowledge and action of the Great Lord (*maheśa*), there is no other cause. (5)

Even material causes such as threads are not observed to produce their own effects without a maker who possesses specific knowledge and activity regarding the cloth and so forth; thus, it is established that every effect whatsoever is pervaded by a mere maker, just as it is pervaded by having a material cause.
Consequently, because the universe possesses a material cause, a maker is proven, just as [the universe] is proven to be preceded by an effect.
There is no inconclusiveness. 4–5.
Now, from the perspective of the Mīmāṃsakas, there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*):
Another says: "The manifold variety of the world must arise from karma due to its diversity;
and since the fruit for persons comes from karma, what role is there here for a Creator? (6)

Since it is an effect, only an agent must be inferred in that case. Furthermore, you yourselves have accepted that action, consisting of merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*), is what produces an effect—just like agricultural labor and the like; so what else remains to be inferred? (6)
This is true; nevertheless, this karma, though observed to be insentient like agriculture and other such activities, depends upon an intelligent agent.

Even observed actions such as agriculture and the like are not seen to produce results without an intelligent agent; they are not capable of bringing about enjoyments for men by themselves. Therefore, since action—even that consisting of merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*)—is an action, it requires one endowed with superior knowledge to bestow its own fruit; rather, this [argument] establishes that very creator of the universe whose existence was previously unproven. Thus, it is not [the case that the argument fails].
The [fault of] proving what is already established: since that [object] is perceived, it is not logical to postulate an unperceived [cause]. || 7 ||
Others say that the creator, joined with many conscious beings, would be the seed through men alone; that it is not by Hara—that is not so.

Just as in the case of physical activities such as agriculture and the like, the seed of the world—consisting of all effects beginning with the *kalās*—will be joined by many conscious persons who are already perceived, acting through their multiplicity as agents.

Thus, because this would involve both the abandonment of what is observed and the postulation of what is unobserved, no other agent is established. Therefore, the phrase "that is not" means that it is not tenable. || 8 ||

Since the cause for men’s production of effects such as the *kalās* and their instruments is either merely the connection between those two—prakṛti and puruṣa—or a specific connection characterized by the relationship of the enjoyed and the enjoyer; in that regard:
if the general connection between those two were the cause of their production...
Consequently, it would follow that the effects beginning with *kalā* are produced eternally. (9)

Because Prakṛti and Puruṣa are all-pervasive, they remain conjoined even in the state of liberation (kaivalya); thus, since their mere relationship persists, there would follow the undesirable consequence that liberation is impossible as long as the production of effects and instruments such as *kalā* continues. || 9 ||
Now, as for the second position: if their conjunction is qualified [by something], its cause must be stated;
for nowhere is any effect ever seen to be without a cause. (10)

For *prakṛti* is not an object of enjoyment by virtue of its own nature as *prakṛti*, nor is the *puruṣa* an enjoyer by virtue of his own nature, because that would entail the impossibility of liberation. Rather, it is through the medium of the effects beginning with *kalā*; for their connection arises from the production of *kalā* and the rest. Therefore, an agent must be asserted for that specific relationship—which is produced, consists of conjunction, and takes the form of the enjoyed and the enjoyer—between those two.
By this it has been stated that an effect cannot possibly exist without a creator. || 10 ||
Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that agency belongs to those two alone here; what need is there for another? This is not so, because:
the Puruṣa does not, by himself, go toward the seed [of action] with respect to him.
This is because the Puruṣa is devoid of power, and because Prakṛti is not seen to possess the capacity to independently fashion the collection of effects and instruments.
Since primordial nature (*prakṛti*) is not perceived, it might be thought that such an instrument for action would exist for the person (*puruṣa*) solely on account of karma;
however, due to the absence of knowledge, there is no agency in the relationship between the experiencer and the non-experiencer, but rather merely a connection.
Therefore, whether in union or in separation, Maheśa is the cause of both.
Therefore, since the means for attaining both worldly enjoyment and liberation cannot otherwise be accounted for, the Supreme Lord alone is the omniscient creator and none other. || 11 ||
In this regard, another [opponent] from the Lokāyata school says:
"Even if you go far, what is the use of Hara as the creator of the world, if the seed of the world exists by its own nature (*svabhāva*)? You must simply state that it is nature itself. (12)
Even having postulated a Supreme Lord, you must further postulate for him the nature of being the creator of the world.

It would be better, therefore, to postulate that very nature of being the creator of the world for *prakṛti*, which is established for both disputants. In this way, many unseen things (*adṛṣṭa*) will not have to be postulated. || 12 ||
That is even more improper; for what is the nature of that creator of the world, characterized as primordial matter (*prakṛti*), to be understood?

Of what specific kind is the nature of the world-maker? [Objection: But is this not a question regarding that which is already defined by the characteristic of being the creator of the world? [Response: True, but—
O wise ones, is activity that of one impelled by another, or rather that of one who is independent? (13)
The nature of that [world]—which has the cause of the world as its essence—is it impelled by an intelligent agent, or is it independent? Regarding this:
it has already been established that there is no evidence for the position that it is independent;
furthermore, it has already been established previously that there is no proof for the position that an insentient thing possesses agency.
How is this established? Because that which produces an effect must be independent; for a non-conscious entity can never be a material cause [of anything]. (14)
Now, as for the second [alternative], that too is indeed logical:
the activity of one endowed with wisdom, impelled by the power of wisdom, is accomplished by the mind;
it is the activity of the wise one, impelled by the power of action (*kriyāśakti*), in the creation of the world. Of him—
Since it is established by valid means of cognition, it is indeed accepted.
And therefore:
"He who is the wise impeller of that [unmanifest] is to be known as the Lord (Īśvara). (15)
Since that which impels [the world] by its own power is an intelligent being, it is established that he alone is God; thus, this is not the doctrine of inherent nature (*svabhāvavāda*).
If this is so, let there be only the power of action as the impeller here—what is the use of a God? For even his status as an agent cannot be established without that [power]. As they say:
"O Caṇḍī, salutations to you, who are the power of action belonging to the Creator; without whom even He possesses no capacity for creation.
Thus, the Supreme Power is established as the power of will; there is no other Lord. (15)
That which proceeds due to its predominance during the day and at night.
At the end of time, she remains asleep here in the inactive ocean of the world;

for it is that very power, having Prakṛti as its substratum, which, following the impulse from Māyā—characterized by an overflowing capacity—proceeds to create the universe. Thus, there is no other Lord. || 16 ||
That is incorrect;
for its cause in the state of excess is none other than Maheśvara.
It has been stated that an insentient entity possesses no capacity for either spontaneous activity or non-activity;
therefore, by the principle of "impossibility otherwise" (anyathānupapatti), the Supreme Lord alone, endowed with a preeminent consciousness, is the cause of its manifestation. || 17 ||
But surely she herself will be omniscient— if she is indeed omniscient, there is dispute only over the name and not over the reality.
If this is so, and since a difference in names does not entail a difference in the reality, then her distinction [from others] remains intact.
Let it be merely conceptualized; in that case, the Vedāntins maintain that the very primordial nature (prakṛti), characterized by attributes such as omniscience, is the Lord (īśvara).
From the Great Lord, who is both self and other, and who possesses the powers of vision and action; || 18 ||
The universe, consisting of both sentient and insentient beings, arises through the distinction between the enjoyer and the enjoyed;
what purpose, then, would there be for a Lord of the World other than that? (19)

And that very one, the omnipresent Lord, is accepted as the sole enjoyer. From the effect characterized as the universe— which is divided by the distinctions of enjoyer and enjoyed, and which consists of the sentient and the insentient— it is inferred that there exists, by way of its effects, a single,
non-dual reality endowed with all knowledge and action, whose nature comprises the enjoyer, the enjoyed, and so forth.

Since the non-dualist position establishes that the material cause—designated as the Supreme Self and characterized as the Lord—is to be inferred, the postulation of a separate, distinct Lord is not tenable. || 18-19 ||

[Objection: Is it not the case that the status of being an effect is unestablished for conscious entities (*cetana*), since their eternality was previously demonstrated in the section on experience? [Reply:

No, because the possibility of being an effect exists due to their being associated with multiple things. Just as in the case of unconscious things, the material cause of conscious things is indeed established as conscious, owing to the association with consciousness (*cit*). [Objection: That too is untenable, because—
If the origin of the world of sentient and insentient beings proceeds from the Self, then that [Self] as well—indeed.
Since the effect, consisting of both consciousness and unconsciousness, arises from that which possesses the attributes of its cause,

if the entire universe— both sentient and insentient— is produced from the Supreme Self, then that Supreme Self must also possess the nature of both sentience and insentience; for effects invariably follow the essential nature of their material cause.
For it is established that specific forms of effects—such as jars produced from gold, clay, and so forth—exist [prior to their manifestation]. || 20 ||
And therefore:
"Two contradictory properties, existing at the same time, have come to reside in a single substratum. (21)
Because they mutually destroy one another, those two effect the annihilation of their own selves.

Since two contradictory things can only achieve their own existence through the mutual suppression of each other—just like a jar and its absence—it is impossible for the conscious and the unconscious to coexist in a single place at a single time. Now, suppose this [self] were conscious in some part...

It is said that it is not by anything; for if it were thus possessed of homogeneity (*sabhāgatva*), then, like a jar or similar objects, it would be an effect, and therefore its status as the supreme cause would be untenable.
Moreover:
"Because it is a material cause, like clay, the Supreme Self would not be conscious. (22)

Since it is certain that material causes such as clay and so forth are insentient, the Supreme Self must also be insentient because it is a material cause; or else, if it were sentient, it could not be a material cause. || 22 ||
Furthermore:
"And those who experience [pleasure and pain] also arise from that [the body], because they are produced, like a jar or similar objects.
It is established that whatever is produced from a material cause (upādānakāraṇa), such as a jar or the like, is indeed insentient.

According to your view, since the individual selves (*ātman*) arise from the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) as their material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*), it follows that these experiencing selves would also be insentient. However, these selves are conscious; they are established through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) by virtue of being both subjects and objects of cognition. Therefore, they are not produced [from a cause], but like the Supreme Self, they are eternal. [Objection: But was it not stated, on the basis of positive concomitance (*anvaya*), that these [selves] possess the nature of an effect, just like insentient things?

That is not tenable, because there is no logical concomitance (*ananvaya*). Furthermore, the self cannot be the object of its own apprehension, because in that case there would be a contradiction regarding its own activity. Rather, we have already explained at length in the commentary on the *Paramokṣanirāsakārikā* that it always manifests as the nature of the immediate subject (*pratyagrūpa*) precisely as the grasper; this should be understood from that very work.
And therefore:
"The Supreme Self possesses the property of producing non-conscious matter, just like clay and other such substances. (23)
Since it has been stated that the Supreme Self is insentient by virtue of being the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*),
it must therefore be admitted— just like clay and other materials— that it is impelled by an intelligent agent for the sake of producing its own effects. //23//
Thus, non-duality is untenable; therefore, the enjoyer, the seed of the world, and the Great Lord are likewise possessed of power. (24)
Each must be determined separately for the sake of pacifying the aforementioned defects.

Therefore, the enjoyer must be admitted as unarisen, the storehouse of the world as insentient, and the creator of the world, Maheśvara, as endowed with attributes such as omniscience; these must be accepted as mutually distinct and eternal.

As it is stated in the *Tattvatrayanirṇaya*: "Śambhu, Puruṣa, and Māyā—this triad of principles remains eternally pervasive and endowed with the power of agency; even when the transformations have fallen asleep, this triad stays awake. Thus, there is no fault whatsoever, as the Supreme Lord is established as distinct from the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*).

[Objection: But power (*śakti*) is immutable; how then can a distinction between knowledge and action be established for the power of Śiva? Even that [distinction] is not real. For it is said: "The power of the Wielder of the Trident is one alone, consisting of all knowledge and action. (25)

If, however, the power of action were distinct from the power of knowledge, then—due to its insentience and because of its transformation into the divisions of Vāmā and so forth—it would not possess an inherence in the Lord, just as Māyā does not; for that [power] is unchanging.
Thus, the Lord would result in being a non-agent due to being devoid of the power of action. And the creation of the universe is not possible without an agent.

Thus, one must necessarily admit the identity of the powers of omniscience and action. [Objection: But surely, since the object of knowledge (*jñeya*) and the effect (*kārya*) are distinct, how can there not be a distinction between the powers? [Reply: No, because even those two are non-distinct. For being an object of knowledge (*jñeyatva*) does not transcend being an effect (*kāryatā*);
for if that were the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the thing itself, it would follow that everyone would be omniscient. Nor does being an effect transcend being an object of knowledge.
There is no real distinction between the powers of knowledge and action; rather, it is merely an imagined one. || 25 ||
In the same way, action is threefold; the power beginning with Vāmā is said to be so by virtue of the difference in its functions.
Even the power of action beginning with Vāmā is divided into three types only through the difference in its functions and is thus proclaimed, but not in reality—namely, Vāmā.

"Jyeṣṭhā, Raudrī, and Śakti—these three powers follow after that. Otherwise, because there would be a distinction based on the distinction of the objects of knowledge, and by the assumption of a distinct cognizer for each object, it would follow that cognition differs with every atom; consequently, the consequence of their being devoid of self-nature (nairātmya) would arise. Just as the perception of multiple objects occurs through a single [cognition] alone...

That which is established through experience can be manifested by the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*); likewise, the performance of manifold effects by the power of action (*kriyāśakti*), when it is in a state of active exertion, is established as uncontradicted. Thus, even the distinction between them is merely conceptualized based on the difference in their functions.
If so, how is there a distinction between the functions? It is said:
"The Great Lord obstructs the impure persons by means of action. (26)
Therefore, He impels those who are bound by beginningless impurity and joined with karma.

First, by His power of action (*kriyā-śakti*), the Lord obstructs and restrains the individual souls (*paśus*) who are possessed of beginningless impurity; subsequently, He impels those who have been thus restrained in accordance with the ripening of their karma. || 26 ||
[Objection: But since they are all-pervasive, how can there be any impelling of them? [Reply: True; however— "From that, for those who have been impelled by the Lord, a great trembling arises. (27)
The capacity for connection with the means of experience is the craving for enjoyment.

Due to their distinction from those who are *vijñānakevalin* (isolated by knowledge), the production of the capacity for the relationship between cause and effect in them according to their karma is precisely what is called "impulsion by the Lord. || 27 ||
Then, however—when the Lord of Knowledge (Vidyeśa), Ananta, abides within the Self as the presiding authority over both the pure and the impure; || 28 ||

Manifested, the Lord agitates the seed of the universe and creates the world. Having impelled Ananta—the Lord of the Mantreśas, who possesses both pure and impure authority—and making him the agent, He brings forth the world from Māyā. As it is heard: "The Sovereign Lord of the Kings of Knowledge causes the world to revolve by His will. (28)
And thereafter—
having united those lustful persons with this world— 29.
For the sake of their experience, the Lord brings about a state consisting of the means of action;
having joined those bound souls (paśus) with bodies and organs according to their karma, the Lord brings about a state consisting of the means for the sake of their experience. (29)
And then:
at the end of the duration of this world, he too [is present] for the sake of rest for those who are rushing through saṃsāra. (30)
And for the sake of producing forbearance in both animals and human beings, the Blessed One then ordains the withdrawal of all [restrictions]. || 31 ||
The functions characterized by abiding, preservation, bestowing, and existence are said to be distinct. || 30–31 ||
He also bestows grace:
"At the end of the obstruction caused by one's own impurity and limited power, he releases [the soul] by the power of initiation alone.
That is to say, when—as will be explained—the authority of the obstruction of both impurity and the Lord’s power ceases, then...
By initiation alone, he liberates the bound souls.
Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Raudrī—though she is inherently non-different [from the One], she is threefold.
Action is divided into three types by its functions: obstruction (*rodha*), separation (*viśleṣa*), and removal (*haraṇa*).

Now, since the activities characterized by maintenance (*sthiti*) and protection (*saṃrakṣaṇa*) have as their fruit the cessation of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*), obstruction is the function of Vāmā; withdrawal (*saṃhāra*), which consists of taking away (*ādāna*), is the function of Jyeṣṭhā; and grace (*anugraha*), which consists of the removal of fetters (*pāśa*), is the function of Raudrī.

By these [names] such as Raudrī and so forth, the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*), though not distinct from Him by its own nature, is said to be divided; yet, in the ultimate sense, there is no fault, for "the power of the Trident-bearer is one alone, consisting of all knowledge and action" (Mokṣopāya 25). || 32 ||
Thus has the status of the God of gods as the creator of all been declared. (33)
By this [reasoning], the Lord is attained as omniscient through His being the maker of all;
for, as was stated previously, since we do not observe the agency of weavers and others without knowledge, the Lord’s omniscience is established by virtue of His being the maker of all.
For it is thus:
[the agent] is endowed with the material cause, the efficient cause, and the fruit. || 34 ||
Just as a weaver recognizes a cloth, so does existence (bhava), which is endowed with the causes of grasping (upādāna) and with its fruit. || 35 ||
The creator of all knows all that exists exactly as it is;

just as a weaver, endowed with stainless knowledge of the three periods of time, produces a cloth from threads for Devadatta by means of a loom and other tools for the sake of obtaining payment, and thus succeeds in his task, so too does the creator of the universe [act] through *māyā*.

Since He is inferred to be endowed with stainless knowledge of the three times while producing the universe—characterized by diverse karma—for the sake of the enjoyment and liberation of bound souls (paśu) as His own effect, His omniscience is established. || 34–35 ||
Thus, because it accomplishes all purposes, the power within the self is twofold.
That power, eternally established, appears like a mass of sparks;
joined with which Maheśāna knows and acts as everything. (37)
Therefore, he is called "possessing parts" (*sakala*) by those who know the truth.

As previously stated, that very Power (*śakti*), whose nature consists of all-knowingness and all-action, though eternal, appears as if manifold; being metaphorically designated as the body of the Lord, Śiva is thus called "possessing parts. (36–37)
But he alone—unbound by the connection to the *kalās* and the *piṇḍas*—is bound in the manner of a bound soul (*paśu*). (38)
At no time is the Lord of Gods [perceived] as such; rather, He is praised as *niṣkala* (partless).
Because He lacks a body composed of *kalās* and other elements—like a bound soul (*paśu*)—the Blessed One is said to be *niṣkala*, as was stated previously.
Here, the opponent [objects]: "But surely, if he is partless (niṣkala), there can be neither knowledge nor agency. (39)

Since the possession of knowledge and so forth is observed only in those bound souls (paśus) who are endowed with a collection of *kalās*, and since the Lord is devoid of such *kalās* and the like, it follows that He lacks knowledge and the rest. || 39 ||
This is not a fault:
"The two [powers], being well-established, require connection with *kalā* for the sake of manifesting consciousness. (40)
Vision and action are obstructed by impurity (mala) in the case of the Lord [of the individual soul], not because of any obstruction on the part of the Lord himself.

For it is stated in the *Bhogaprakaraṇa*: "The knowledge and action of bound souls (paśus), being obstructed by impurity, proceed toward objects only in dependence upon the manifesting factors such as *kalā*. However, for the Supreme Lord, these two do not exist, because He is unobstructed from time immemorial.
"Dependent upon manifestors" means [it would have to be perceived] at all times and regarding all objects. (40)
Even for the Lord, since He is dependent [on other factors],
His powers of perception and action— due to His being ignorant [in that regard]— are like those of a bound soul (paśu), as they depend on the manifestation of the kalās and other principles.
If it is thus, then he becomes a bound soul (paśu). || 41 ||
Due to the connection with the *kalās* and other [categories], the Lord would result in being a bound soul (*paśu*), just like Devadatta and others. || 41 ||
Or let it be so; what loss is there for us?
For, since no effect can exist without a Lord, a Lord other than that [effect] must be asserted.
Since an effect characterized as the universe does not arise without a Lord, therefore a Lord distinct from it must be asserted.
Thus, there is an infinite regress.
If, even after creating the constituent parts (kalās), he were to perform the action while still joined with them, then [the following would apply].
For this very reason, it is said that the Lord, having created his own effects such as *kalā* and the rest, and being then joined with them, performs all activity. || 42 ||
If this is so—

since vision and action are held to belong to the partless (niṣkala) [Lord]— what is the purpose of the kalās? Just as He, being independent of the kalās and the rest, is indeed partless and yet effects the functions of His own self, in the very same way, He effects the universe as well.
"What is the purpose of postulating for him a body consisting of parts such as the *kalās*?"—this and other points have been explained in detail in the *Nareśvaraparīkṣā*.
Therefore, enough with this digression; [this is] that which accomplishes both enjoyment and liberation. || 43 ||
This Maheśāna, possessing the characteristics already described, is to be worshipped by those seeking liberation.

Since He alone—the Supreme Lord, characterized by omniscience and other such qualities—is the bestower of liberation from the state of bondage (paśu), He alone should always be propitiated by those desiring the highest good, and no other. Thus has been explained enjoyment along with its means. || 43 ||
Now, liberation along with its means is described:
Liberation is the severance of the bonds such as impurity (mala) and the arising of all-encompassing knowledge and action. (44)
Liberation is its effect; Śambhu is the agent; the Lord’s own power is the instrument;
and because it is that which is being liberated, the fivefold self is considered the object of the action. (45)

Because [the soul] is eternally liberated, that which is called liberation consists in the removal of the forms of karma. Previously, in the section on experience (*bhoga-prakaraṇa*), it was established that for those who are *vijñānakevalins*, there is only impurity (*mala*); for those who are *pralayakevalins*, there is both impurity and karma; but for the *sakalas* (conditioned souls), the fetters (*pāśas*) of the bound ones (*paśus*) are characterized by impurity, karma, and *māyā*. Among these...

Liberation for souls is the severance of all bonds as they arise, along with the manifestation of omniscience and omnipotence; it is not, as in other systems, the severance of only one particular bond, nor is it ignorance, non-agency, or transmigration—as we shall explain later. Furthermore, for that liberation, the self is not something to be known [as an object].

As in such cases, this bound soul (*paśu*) is the agent; for since the bound soul is always the object (*karman*) due to being consecrated by the Lord (*īśvara*), [the agent] is not *prakṛti* or other such bonds, but rather the Lord himself. And His instrument is His own power, known as initiation (*dīkṣā*). Liberation (*mukti*) consists of the severing of the bonds and the manifestation of omniscience and other qualities; thus, liberation is a specific state residing in the one to be liberated, and not—

This would be like the position of the Sāṃkhyas regarding the one who is liberated, because since that [Self] is eternally liberated, it would follow that there is no distinction between liberation and non-liberation. As they say: "Prakṛti causes transmigration through its state as an object of experience, but by ceasing that, she grants liberation. This is not a loss of the Self itself, nor does the person know it for himself. Thus, whether qualified or unqualified, all liberation here consists of this very thing.
Having been thus proposed, the subsequent section provides its proof. 44–45.
In this regard, first of all, those among our own school who maintain that liberation consists in knowledge [assert] that liberation is indeed produced by human effort:
"Let liberation belong to the self, for like experience, it therefore pertains to the person (pudgala). (46)
Discrimination (*viveka*) and the like, which bring about liberation, are established as the means;

let the Lord (*īśvara*) be the creator of the universe, yet human beings experience pleasant and unpleasant results through their own performed merits and demerits (*dharma-adharma*), not through those created by the Lord. [Objection: But even in that case, the Supreme Lord certainly possesses the status of a presiding controller (*adhiṣṭhātṛ*). [Reply: Let it be so; however, no.
Furthermore, because they are bound by the impurity of ignorance, those very souls, through delusion, partake in saṃsāra;

yet, upon the cessation of ignorance through the arising of discerning knowledge purified by the practice of its antidote, they attain the state of omniscience and other qualities. Thus, liberation is brought about by their own selves as the agents, not by God as the agent. (46)
That is incorrect:
ignorance arising from non-discriminative ascertainment is what is removed. (47)
Nothing other than the knowledge of discrimination can be the cause for the cessation of substances such as glass;
it ceases only through the cessation of its own cause, and not otherwise. (48)
If impurity were caused by ignorance, then in its state as ignorance it would be insubstantial.
Alternatively, if it were an existent property of the self, it would cease upon [the realization of] its insubstantiality. (49)
Knowledge and the like, being fruitless for the person, are excluded by virtue of their being [mere] dharmas;
if they were to be excluded, they would not be the attributes of the self, and thus that which obstructs them would be beginningless. (50)
Therefore, by means of that initiation, there is the cessation of the impurity of the conscious self;
thus, that individual soul (aṇu) is no longer subject to the impurity of Maheśa, māyā, and the rest, through its own self.
How will he liberate himself from them, since he does not possess the power to liberate himself? (52)
Through them, one comes under the control of the fetters; therefore, the Lord is the master who grants liberation.

It is logical that men are the agents of merit and demerit, because their power of knowledge and action (*dṛkkriyā*) has been stimulated by the slight removal of impurity (*mala*) through the [categories] beginning with *kalā*, due to their connection with those [principles]. But when the cessation of impurity and so forth occurs, then even the state of omniscience arises.
To say that those for whom lordship (*īśvaratva*) has not been seen to be capable [of it] will attain liberation is an extreme rashness. [Objection:

But surely, in cases such as the error of silver in mother-of-pearl, the cessation of ignorance through knowledge is established by valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*). [Response: It is incorrect to claim that impurity (*mala*) is ignorance (*ajñāna*) and that it exists beginninglessly in relation to the selves (*ātman*), because such a thing cannot logically be ignorance. Not so.
Ignorance (*ajñāna*) is not the impurity itself, but rather the cause of impurity. If it were ignorance, it would have to be either an attribute of the Self or something insubstantial (*tuccha*).

If it were insubstantial, it would be incapable of producing any effect, and thus knowledge and other means intended to remove it would be fruitless. If, on the other hand, it were an attribute of the Self, then—just like its eternality or all-pervasiveness—it could not be removed, resulting in the impossibility of liberation (*anirmokṣa*). If it were removable, it could not be an attribute of the Self.

It is indeed a different entity. Since it is the cause of the self's beginningless obstruction, ignorance must be described as a defect, like a cataract or similar film over the eye. Furthermore, the cessation of a substance that is the cause of ignorance—whether it be a cataract or something else—is not observed through knowledge, because there is no state of opposition between them. How, then, is there cessation through knowledge in cases such as [the perception of] silver in a mother-of-pearl shell? It is said: [ignorance] is of two kinds.

Now, ignorance (*ajñāna*) consists of: (1) the cognition of silver and the like with respect to mother-of-pearl and the like, which is characterized by the non-discriminative determination of a similarity previously experienced;
and (2) conceptual cognition (*vikalpajñāna*) whose objects are double moons and the like, produced by substances such as cataracts or jaundice.
Among these, the former ceases through the knowledge of discriminative determination, namely, "This is not silver. As for that [ignorance] which is produced by substances, its...

Cessation occurs only through the cessation of its own causal substance, not through knowledge. It has been established that ignorance belongs to the selves solely as having substance as its cause, and nothing else, because that [ignorance] is non-spiritual (abauddha); therefore, its cessation is not possible through knowledge. Just as cataracts and the like are removed by an oculist and so forth, its cessation is brought about by Īśvara alone; thus, it is the work of Īśvara alone.

Liberation is not something produced by the self. Thus it is stated in another branch [of scripture]: "The liberation of souls comes from Śiva alone. The Śruti also says: "He whom this [Lord] chooses, by him He is attained" (Kaṭhopaniṣad 2.23; Muṇḍakopaniṣad 3.2.3). For this very reason, because it is not something to be accomplished through action—as is the case with material objects—liberation is said to be brought about solely by the activity of the Lord: "Initiation alone delivers one upward to the state of Śiva."
"He leads [the soul] even to the abode," as we shall explain [later]. (47–52)

[Objection: Surely, even if one postulates that the Lord is the agent of liberation, one must further postulate that His nature is the removal of the fetters (*pāśa*), for without that [nature], He too would not be established as such. Consequently, those very fetters, being removed by virtue of His nature, will become the cause of the person's liberation; what is the use of postulating the Lord’s agency? [Reply: That is incorrect, because—
Even the nooses do not possess the power to liberate men.

Since it is observed that [the Lord] himself binds with a rope or the like and then releases them, it has been stated that the individual soul (jīva) possesses no inherent capacity for either engagement or withdrawal. Therefore, since Śiva alone is the one who removes even the fetters (pāśas) at that time, He is the bestower of liberation to souls; and when this is seen, there is no need to postulate an unseen force (adṛṣṭa). || 53 ||
Regarding this, the opponent says: "The fetters cause the manifestation of [the soul's] cognition and agency in manifold ways. (54)
Liberation is the manifestation of those two alone; therefore, liberation is brought about by the fetters (*pāśa*).

For it is observed that the fetters, characterized as the body and the organs, produce in the self during the state of transmigratory existence a manifestation of knowledge and agency of many kinds. And liberation is the manifestation of knowledge and action.
Therefore, since those very [factors] whose efficacy has been observed will bring about even that [result], what is the use of postulating an unobserved Īśvara there?
This is incorrect:
for the fetters bind one who is colored by their own forms and who is attached to the functioning of the fetters.

Driven by worldly existence, they manifest the manifestation of those two [the intellect and the ego], which are characterized by sequential order, intended for destruction, contradictory, and have a vast range, because they are devoid of consciousness.
Because it is incapable of being called "liberation," it is distinct from that [liberation].

For whatever manifesting agent, such as a lamp, is established as possessing the power to manifest a thing exactly as it is, that same kind of power is inferred even in another case where the object is unperceived. And this [power] is characterized by its capacity for producing effects and so forth.

The manifestor, though impelled by the Lord as previously described, acts as the cause for the grasping of a self within the body and so forth; it manifests the knowledge and activity of living beings— which is colored by its own form, attached to objects such as women, directed toward various objects at various times and places, obstructed by passion, hatred, and the like, and perishable upon the destruction of the body and other effects— due to the fact that these [effects] are produced.

The statement "it is seen" establishes that its status as a manifestor (vyañjaka) pertains precisely to an object that is already such [as it appears]; it does not arise from an absolute difference [between the object and the cognition].

Therefore, just as a lamp [manifests] the universe, even in liberation there is no liberation manifested by the fetters; thus, it is said that the distinction of knowledge and action exists in liberation. || 55–56 ||
The power that overcomes the bonds is called *dṛk* (vision) and *kriyā* (action) in the case of the perfected ones (*siddhas*).
Therefore, he does not indulge in passion for a wife arising from the snare-net;
for the perfected one (siddha), whose power consists of knowledge and action is like that of the Lord due to the cessation of all bonds, his power destroys the snares.
Thus, unlike the bound soul (paśu), he does not indulge in the attachment of grasping the body and so forth as the self, which is manifested by the snares.
For she is not pierced by nooses, whether they have arisen or have perished. || 58 ||
Therefore, the power (śakti) is not at all constrained by the activities of the fetters (pāśa);

nor is that perfected power (siddha-śakti)—which, unlike the bound soul (paśu), is not constrained by the activities of the fetters such as passion (rāga) and the like, and which remains attached to objects such as women—constrained, because it persists even during the dissolution of the fetters with its very own unmodified nature, just like the power of the Lord (īśvara-śakti). || 58 ||
Moreover:
"That power has all things as its object; it is not, for that very reason, of limited scope. (59)
Because she manifests simultaneously in all objects of knowledge and actions, she is not sequential.

Due to the absence of obscuration, she always and everywhere effects the cognition of all that is to be known and performs all actions; unlike the power of the bound soul (paśu), she is never limited to a particular object at a particular time or place.
And that [cognition] is not sublated by another individual [cognition], because no other individual [cognition] appears.

Nor is that perfected power (siddha-śakti) sublated by another manifestation characterized as supreme liberation, as is the case with the manifestation of power among the Vidyeśvaras; for, due to its equality with Śiva, there is no further excellence beyond it. || 60 ||
Furthermore—
once it has begun to function, it does not obstruct [the soul] equally with respect to the object of knowledge and its duty;
nor does it proceed toward or withdraw from an effect by the will of Īśvara, as is the case with the powers of the Vidyeśvaras, because [the soul] is equal to Śiva.
Because the state of being impelled by God has ceased entirely for one whose power is perfected, since he possesses power inherently.
The snares do not manifest that [state], nor is one overcome by them again. || 61 ||
Because their seeds have been scorched by the will of Śiva, that power [of the soul] is imperishable;
it is not manifested through the bonds (pāśas) and the body-instruments (kāryakaraṇa) as is the case with the bound soul (paśu-śakti) described below,
nor is it ever again overwhelmed by those bonds whose seeds have been burnt, once it has been manifested by the power of Śiva.

Therefore, the manifestation of the perfected power (siddha-śakti) is not perishable, unlike the manifestation of the power of bound souls (paśu-śakti); thus, in another manner, the perishability [of the manifestation] is avoided.
The manifestation of that which is to be manifested (vyaṅgya-vyakti) lasts only as long as the presence of the manifestor (vyañjaka-saṃnidhi). || 62 ||
It is said that this principle exists when the power is perfected, and does not exist otherwise;
for the Śiva-power is that which brings about manifestation through its proximity.
Even because of this, the Creator does not constantly perceive [the effect];
for it was stated previously that the presiding over by God (īśvarādhiṣṭhāna) of the perfected beings (siddhas) is entirely absent.
Therefore, due to the lack of presiding by a manifestor—just as a lamp does not preside over it—the manifestation ceases, just like a jar or similar objects.

[It would follow that the power] is indeed perishable. This is not a fault, because the Supreme Lord is not intended as the manifester of the power by merely effecting a non-permanent removal of the veil of the manifested object—as is the case with a lamp—whereby this fault would arise.
Rather, He effects a permanent removal of the veils, like an oculist for the eyes, thereby [manifesting] for the perfected ones a power identical to His own.

Since it brings into manifestation the Śaiva power of vision and action—which makes manifest the potency of the Siddhānta through its union with the Siddhas and Śivas—how could there be any need for another manifestor of it? For, like the power of Śiva, it is by its very nature omniscient. Not only is it unmanifested by bonds (*pāśas*), but for this reason as well, it is not subject to destruction.

For this very reason, impermanence does not follow from being an effect, because liberation is something manifested (*vyaṅgya*). Since it is the manifestation—through the removal of obstructions—of the power of knowledge and so forth that was already previously established, it possesses omniscience rather than being merely a state of abiding in one's own nature; thus, liberation is said to be distinct from everything else. (62–63)
Thus, for you whose perfected power is of such a distinct nature, there are no fetters.

For it is capable of manifesting [the power] because [this manifestation] occurs through their cessation. It has been stated that since the power of the bound soul (*paśu-śakti*) is manifested by bonds (*pāśa-vyaṅgyā*), it is entirely distinct from the power of the perfected Śiva (*siddha-śiva-śakti*) which exists even in the absence of bonds;
thus, the manifestation of the power of the liberated one by means of bonds is not established. Therefore, the Lord (*īśvara*) alone is its manifester.
It is the cause of liberation. || 64 ||

Now, the Sāṃkhya may argue that since "Yoga is the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind" (Yoga Sūtra 1.2), it is the internal organ alone, refined by yoga and other means, that is the cause of liberation for the selves, and not the Lord; but that is incorrect—for yoga, knowledge, austerity, and the exertion of means for experience [all depend on Him]. (65)
According to the logic previously stated, because it is a bond (*pāśa*), it cannot be the means for its own liberation;

furthermore, because the mind is insentient (*jaḍa*) as already described, it is like the wind—it cannot function on its own even when refined by yoga and other practices. Thus, *māyā* must be made to evolve by the Self (*ātman*), and not otherwise. If [the Self] were to cease due to the absence of discrimination (*viveka*), it would either cease forever, or else [it would never cease].

If liberation were only "at some time," there would be no liberation at all; or else, liberation would belong to the self at all times. Furthermore, who here is the practitioner of yoga and so forth for whom the instruction of the treatise is intended? It cannot be the self, because you yourselves have accepted it as being devoid of activity (*niṣkriya*).
Nor can it be the mind (*citta*), because it is insentient (*jaḍa*). (65)
Moreover:
"Even the most intense means do not cause the destruction of one's own self. (66)
Since even an extremely sharp sword-blade does not cut its own self,

the practice of yoga and other disciplines for the sake of suppressing the mind's own activity is not possible by itself, because of the contradiction of an action operating upon its own self. Therefore, it follows that the Lord alone is the cause of both engagement and cessation, and thus the cause of liberation in all cases.

Now, one might ask: why does even the Lord not become the cause of liberation for all beings simultaneously? It is because He has no requirements [to fulfill]. It is not due to a dependence on the ripening of impurity (*mala*), for otherwise the observed regularity [of experience] would be untenable. As it has been said: "When that [impurity] is exhausted, there arises the desire to go toward supreme liberation" (Svacchanda Tantra 32.17). Impurity, however, possesses such an inherent nature.

If it is conceived [as a transformation], then because it is insentient (*jaḍa*), its transformation in such a manner at some time or for someone does not deserve censure. As it is said in the *Tattvatrayanirṇaya*: "The impurity (*mala*) ceases through suppression, through the power of the Person (*pums*), or through transformation over time;
due to the occurrence of specific transformations, it [ceases] sometimes, for someone, and in some way. (Verse 12) || 66 ||
If it is thus:
"When the time for the individual soul's (aṇu) mastery over the power of obstruction has passed, [it occurs] spontaneously. (67)
But when the impurity has ceased, the remaining multitude of fetters (pāśas) ceases;
upon their cessation, the power of vision and action within the self becomes inherently pure.

Consequently, existence (bhava) does not bring about liberation for men, as it manifests all objects [of experience]. When that cause has ceased of its own accord— due to the ripening of the impurity (mala) through the power of knowledge and other means,
and due to the exhaustion of the period during which it had the authority to obstruct— then, upon the cessation of that cause, there follows the cessation of other bonds (pāśas).
Since their powers of knowledge and action are pure, they will manifest liberation by themselves; what need is there for the agency of God?

Well then, let the Supreme Lord alone, being independent, be the cause of liberation. In that case, this fault does not arise, nor is there the risk of over-extension, because [liberation] is regulated by His own will. As the Lord of Knowledge (Vidyādhipati) said: "This descent of power belonging to Śiva is independent."
"He is the one who effects the liberation of animals; for if he were dependent [on others], the Supreme Lord would be incapable. No, because that [dependence] is impossible. (67–68)
When there is stability, there is no withdrawal; or when there is withdrawal, there is no stability.
Furthermore, the Lord does not always provide enjoyment to one who is devoid of karma.
For if he were independent and thus disregarded karma and other factors, the Lord would— without cause— be constantly engaged in the creation and destruction of the world,
as well as providing enjoyment even to one devoid of karma, granting liberation even through evil deeds, and effecting the destruction of even one who is liberated.

If [the world] were to act thus, it would become as inconsistent as the behavior of a madman; consequently, no one would engage in activity for the sake of enjoyment, liberation, or the avoidance of evil deeds. Thus, since all the instructional scriptures would be rendered useless, the materialist (Lokāyata) alone would be worthy of worship by you. Therefore, in order to avoid such inconsistency, [the Lord] must depend upon the ripening of karma and so forth.

The creator of all must be accepted. And dependence on that [creator] does not constitute a lack of autonomy; rather, it is dependence upon another Lord. Since he has no such dependence upon a Supreme Lord, he alone is autonomous. Given this state of affairs, he never effects destruction and so forth, nor enjoyment and so forth, for one who is devoid of karma without cause; thus, the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) is indeed dependent [on prior causes].

If it is argued that [the Lord] will thus depend upon the equality of karma, we say no. Just as the Lord does not bring about experience for one who lacks karma, so too He does not grant liberation to one who lacks the transformation of impurity (*mala*), because liberation depends upon the transformation of impurity;
otherwise, the postulation of impurity would be purposeless. Furthermore, it was established previously that impurity exists in souls apart from karma.

In the section on enjoyments (Bhogaprakaraṇa), it is stated that for those [souls], there is only the state of being a *vijñānakevalin* due to the transformation of impurity (*mala*) and the destruction of karma.
Therefore, it must necessarily be asserted that the ripening of impurity alone is the cause for the descent of power (*śaktipāta*). || 69 ||

Now, it might be argued that since that impurity (mala) will cease of its own accord through maturation, it will become the cause of liberation for persons; thus, there would be no need for the postulation of the descent of Śiva’s power (śivaśaktinipāta). This has indeed been stated, but it is incorrect, because:
"It is certain that all things, both sentient and insentient, are subject to his control. (70)
For he is the cause of their engagement or withdrawal;
thus, Śiva, having rent asunder the net of bonds of the individual soul with the spear of his power, [acts]. (71)
It manifests the two-fold impurity (mala) which consists of the nature of all-knowing cognition and action.

It has been stated that an insentient entity lacks the capacity for either spontaneous engagement or withdrawal. Therefore, even when fully matured, impurity—being a substance like a cataract or similar obstruction—can only be removed by an intelligent agent; thus, it is the Lord alone who, preceded by the removal of that [impurity], [bestows grace] upon individuals.
Manifesting forms such as omniscience and so forth, nothing other than this is the cause of liberation. || 70-71 ||

Now, as for whether the Lord of all these is the direct cause of liberation for everyone or for some through mediation, the sequence established in the *Ruru-siddhānta* is stated here: "At the beginning of creation, the Lord, by His will, [created] eight [gods], both formless (*niṣkala*) and with form (*sakala*). (72)

At the very commencement of creation, he directly favors eight individuals known by names such as Ananta and others, who possess all [eight] kalās without deficiency; having first severed their fully ripened impurities,
he favors them with liberation characterized by the manifestation of omniscience and omnipotence.

It should be understood that the statement "he makes [them] Lords of Knowledge" (vidyeśvarān karoti) pertains exclusively to the position of the individual souls (aṇupakṣa), and not to the positions of the Śaktis or the Śambhus.
Immediately after this—[he should worship] the seven times ten million [deities], both the partless (niṣkala) and the with-parts (sakala), who are atomic (aṇu). || 73 ||
Therefore, by manifesting the activity of all-encompassing knowledge, the Lord makes the mantras his instruments;
thus, having directly favored those very atoms numbering seventy million, the Blessed One creates the mantras. (73)
Since the Mantras and Mantreśvaras are liberated, is it not the case that they possess equality with Śiva? No; he says:
"But because this [state] is produced from the power of Rudra and is also impelled by him, it is indeed inferior. (74)
The two principles known as Mantra and Mantreśvara have been declared.

Of Rudra, who is Bhava, there are the powers Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Raudrī. Below that power, these two principles characterized as Vidyeśvara and Vidya are to be understood; for by them [the soul] is produced and impelled into its own sphere of authority.

Thus it is stated in the scripture: "Impelled by the will and the ordinance of Śiva. Because they are impelled, even though they possess omniscience, their power of action (*kriyāśakti*) is progressively and partially diminished in comparison to the Supreme Lord due to the presence of residual impurities (*malayoga*). As it is said: "The state of being a Vidyā or Vidyeśvara is a lower liberation; here, [the highest] is equality with Śiva" (Śloka 51).

This is stated in the *Tattvasaṃgraha* and other works: "Because they are inferior to this [Śakti-tattva], these [categories] exist below the Śakti-tattva; however, this is not due to spatial location, because souls (*ātman*) are all-pervading. (74)
For this very reason:
"Above Māyā, because it is partless (niṣkala), that which is above Māyā [is established] by virtue of its authority. (75)
That very [pair] is considered by the wise for the purpose of initiation (*dīkṣā*) in the treatises on the process of emanation (*prakriyāśāstra*).

This pair of principles (*tattva*) is all-pervasive; because it exercises authority above *māyā* and because it is devoid of the effects and instruments beginning with *kalā*, it is recited in the treatises on the paths (*adhvaśāstra*) as being situated above *māyā*. || 75 ||
In the same way,
all those who are younger are to be impelled, as well as those who are the elder impellers.
The mantras are considered to have lords (pati) and non-lords (apatayaḥ), while above them are regarded as the Mantreśvaras.

Because they are the lords of the mantras and because they were produced prior to the mantras, the state of being "above" (ūrdhvam) for Ananta and the other Vidyeśvaras—meaning their superior position relative to those mantras—should be understood. Due to being impelled by them, their [the Vidyeśvaras'] power of action (kriyāśakti) is inferior to that [of the mantras].
[This is] because of the downward orientation of the mantras. || 76 ||
Immediately after that—having created the *kalās* and having joined the individual souls (*pudgalas*) with them, the Great Lord (Maheśāna) [proceeds]. (77)
He bestows grace upon the Lords of Mantra (mantreśas), who are the presiding authorities over the womb of Māyā;

and by means of presiding over the Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśvaras), having brought about the entire creation of the categories (tattva), worlds (bhuvana), and aggregates (piṇḍa) beginning with Kalā from Māyā,
and having joined individual souls (pudgalas) with those [categories] according to their karma, [he acts] from among them...
The Lord directly bestows grace upon those atoms whose impurities have been transformed, by means of [confering] the status of Vidyēśvara, which is the office within the womb of Māyā.
(77) He states what their names are and how many there are:
"The eight lords of the maṇḍalas, as well as the group of eight beginning with Krodheśa. (78)
By his will, he [manifests] the hundred Rudras preceded by Vīrabhadra;
first among the group of eight [Rudras] is Krodheśa, together with Śrīkaṇṭha. Thus it is stated in the *Tattvasaṃgraha*:
"The Maṇḍalins, Śrīkaṇṭhas, Krodhas, and so forth" (verse 30). In this way, there are one hundred and eighteen of them.
He bestows grace upon the Rudras. || 78 ||
For they are the applicators of mantras for the sake of favoring living beings. || 79 ||
Therefore, these are Mantreśvaras and do not abide above the Mantras.

Thus, because they arise after the Mantras and Mantreśvaras, and because they exercise authority over the *māyāgarbha* (the womb of *māyā*), they exist in a lower state; nevertheless, like the Ācāryas and others, they possess the status of Mantreśvara because they employ the Mantras for the sake of bestowing grace upon bound souls (*paśu*).
But this is not so because [the mantra] stands above the mantras, as is the case with Ananta and the others. || 79 ||
Furthermore:
"The previously mentioned mantras are partless (niṣkala), whereas these are characterized differently from them. (80)
Below that level of the reality of Mantra (mantratattva) is the sphere of authority for those within the womb of Māyā (māyāgarbhādhikārin).

Since the Mantras are described as being partless (niṣkala), whereas these [Mantra-īśvaras] possess parts (sakala), their power is inferior even to the former; thus, their sphere of authority lies below, precisely within the womb of Māyā. It is solely due to this difference in authority that the classes of Mantras and Mantra-īśvaras are distinct from one another.

They are indeed distinct from their powers (*śakti*), but they are not the veilers (*āvāraka*). As the author of the *Vārttika* says: "All three of these are without distinction in their supreme form; they differ from one another only due to their association with great or small sources (*yoni*). (80)
It is now stated where the stationing of these [deities], such as Vīrabhadra and others, occurs on the path:
"Because they hold office within the womb of Māyā and because they possess kalās, according to the teaching. (81)
Below that Māyātattva, they are endowed with Śiva and Śakti;

since their authority over the womb of Māyā and their state of being "with parts" (sakala) have been described, their abiding below the Māyātattva—in the worlds beginning with Kalā—is like that of Brahmā and the others. || 81 ||
Now, one might object: since these [entities] possess all parts yet their vision and action are contracted by *kalā* and the other [categories], they are like bound souls (*paśu*);
how then can they be endowed with the power of Śiva within the jurisdiction of Māyā? It is said in reply:
"Even when joined with *kalā*, they are not subject to the *kalās*, unlike the multitude of bound souls. (82)
They, together with the animals, are subject to them;
for they are situated above those [elements], such as Time (Kāla) and the rest, in successive order. (83)

Since those *kalās* are subject to them because they are impelled along with the *paśus*, therefore, even when joined with the *kalās* and so forth, these [deities] do not remain under the control of the *kalās*; thus, their omniscience and their authority over the *māyāgarbha* are not contradictory.
(82) — Along with the *mantras* are their lords; with the higher ones are the others, together with the lower ones.
The authority manifests immediately after the manifestation of its own power.

When the Lord has manifested the corresponding powers of knowledge and action for the Mantreśvaras such as Ananta and others, for the higher [deities] such as the Krodhas, and for the lower ones such as Vīrabhadra and others— preceded by the severing of their bonds— it is only then that they exercise their respective offices. It is not otherwise.
He awaits another time. || 84 ||
As for the mantras:
"For the sake of liberation from the bond of Māyā, he created seven crores of mantras from his own self as the cause; 'seven times seven'—such is the rule according to the Śruti. (85)
The distinction is that their performance of the ritual task occurs at a later time; is that authority of theirs permanent?
It is said: "No—for such [beings] as these, the Mantras and the Lords of Mantras, even though they have already achieved their purpose."
But for those dependent on their professional duties, their entitlement is limited by a specific time. || 86 ||

Even for these who have accomplished their purpose and are liberated, because they remain dependent on activity like cattle, there exists the aforementioned authority which extends until death. || 86 ||
Now, the mutual relationship of primary and secondary among Ananta and the others is also described:
Ananta, the leader of the subtle [principles] and the rest, impelled by Śiva and joined with them, performs the acts of creation, maintenance, withdrawal, concealment, and grace. (87)

Just as Ananta, being inferior to Śiva by virtue of the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*), performs the functions of maintenance and so forth while presided over by Śiva, in the same way, Sūkṣma is [inferior] to Ananta—according to the scripture: "Of them, Ananta is the Supreme Lord" (*Raurava Saṃhitā* 2.12). Likewise, Śivottama is [inferior] to Sūkṣma, and so on for all [the subsequent lords], each in relation to its respective predecessor.
A deficiency is to be understood [here]. || 87 ||

Now, the period of authority for the mantras and their mutual distinctions are being stated: "The first half of the mantras, immediately after the Kṛta age, was uttered by Bhava out of grace, due to the diversity of their respective authorities. (88)
Having granted authority to those men who were honored at that time through the desire to bestow grace as the cause,
he attains the imperishable union with Śiva.

Having previously observed that the cycle of existence— consisting of mantras numbering seventy million— is exceedingly ripe with impurities, afflicted by birth, disease, and the like, and having informed the Lord that we are unable to endure association with that [existence] or our own subjection to the state of bound souls (paśu), solely through His impulsion...

Even without regard for the command of Vidyeśvara, those non-atomic beings (aṇu) were gathered together by the power of Śiva; at that very moment, having been graced by [Śiva] directly through His own agency and intellect as well as through His instruments, and having been assigned various offices, they attained supreme liberation, which is equality with Śiva. (88–89)
What is the account of the second half? It is said:
Śiva created the remaining mantras, their retinues, the limbs, the Śambaras, and the mandalas for the sake of attaining perfection and liberation. (90)

Then, for the sake of setting the remaining half in motion, the Supreme Lord created, for the benefit of the worlds, other atoms surrounded by minute particles, the limbs such as the heart, the union with powers (*śakti*), the *śambara* mantras and the words that denote them, the mandalas which are the places of worship such as the nine-spoked wheel (*navanābha*), and so forth. || 90 ||
Now, regarding these mantras, is their agency in bestowing grace exactly like that of the former ones? No; it is said:
"Those mantras, together with their retinues, ancillaries, and Śambaras, are released by Śambhu, who resides within the Teacher (deśika), once they have been impelled [by him]. (91)

For these [deities], when accompanied by their retinues and so forth, because they are employed by Īśvara in the office of the preceptor during initiation and other rites, they always possess the capacity for bestowing grace, but never possess independent agency. || 91 ||

Below their own respective worlds, these Lords of Mantras (mantreśas), impelled by the power of the Lord (īśa-śakti), bestow both enjoyment and liberation; they grant each [of these] to living beings according to their own [capacity].

The remaining subordinate Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśas), such as Vīrabhadra, Rudra, and others, bestow grace upon living beings both in the worlds prescribed by the scriptures—situated above [the earth]—and in their own respective abodes for certain beings such as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and so forth; however, they are not creators of the manifestation of the worlds and so on, like Ananta and the others. || 92 ||
The limit of the authority of the mantras and the lords of mantras is stated as follows:
"These Rudras, beginning with Sūkṣma, and the mantras, together with Ananta, attain equality with Śiva; at the end of their respective offices, they attain liberation through the grace of Hara. (93)

In this regard, at the very time of Ananta’s supreme dissolution, there occurs the simultaneous attainment of equality with Śiva—the supreme liberation—for all [the lords], including Sūkṣma and the others, as well as their respective lords, Vīrabhadra and the rest.
As it is stated: "At the supreme end of Ananta, for those great sovereigns, the cause of universal agency is ordained."

"The supreme state" (Raurava Sūtra 2.13). For this very reason, it is not attained through a gradual process. As the author of the Vārttika says: "In the infinite supreme place, that subtle one presides over each great soul as they move from step to step; yet Śiva creates another station for Śikhaṇḍin among the Rudras. (93)
Now, it is said when Ananta’s activity ceases:
"Having performed the fivefold acts beginning with creation, Ananta then, being liberated from dependence, attains equality with the Lord (pati). (94)

When, within a single manifestation of Māyā, the fivefold activities— namely the fivefold actions of creation and so forth pertaining to Māyā— are completed by Ananta, then, because the entirety of Māyā’s effects has been withdrawn, Ananta, having accomplished his purpose, attains equality with the Lord (pati) and supreme liberation at the very onset of the great dissolution. || 94 ||

If this is so, since Ananta and the others have been withdrawn, how does the Blessed One create other creations from Māyā? It is said: "In this way, Śaṅkara [acts] throughout past and future creations."
He has liberated other men and will liberate others yet to come. || 95 ||

The meaning is that at each secondary creation (pratisarga), the Blessed One, having first brought about Ananta and the others, and having accomplished the enjoyment (bhoga) of men, effects their liberation (mokṣa). || 95 ||
Thus,
the deity established in the teacher liberates men by the very power of initiation,
through his own power which is accomplished by the practice of mantra, for those who have been presented [to him].

It has been stated that the Supreme Lord himself, abiding in the teacher, liberates those persons whose impurities have been fully ripened by means of initiation—which is accomplished through mantra—from everything other than the mantra and the lords of mantra. || 96 ||

Thus, every point previously asserted—that [liberation] does not occur through knowledge and so forth—has been determined. If this is so, how can there be liberation for those who have been abducted after being anointed with the ointment of *māyā*? For them as well, the Blessed Lord himself, presiding over the teacher (*ācārya*), performs the initiation, since teachers are present in every world-level (*bhuvana*). To illustrate:
The lords of mantras, the gurus, the ancient Rudras, the gods, and the lords of sages—
by the lords of mantras the Rudras were instructed, and by the Rudras the gods were well-instructed.

In this place, the lords of sages are honored by the gods; mortals who are sages are honored by the lords of sages; likewise, humans are honored by humans, and those established in the castes are honored by the best of the twice-born.
The Rudras here are Śrīkaṇṭha and the others. Thus, because Gurus exist, liberation occurs everywhere through initiation solely by virtue of their respective agency. (97–98)
The following, which was stated by the best of the twice-born regarding the arrangement of castes, is now established:
"In this world, all four castes possess the qualification for initiation and for being a practitioner;
however, the office of the Guru is proclaimed to belong to the Brāhmaṇa alone. (99)

Regarding the initiation of the practitioner (*sādhaka-dīkṣā*) and so forth, Brāhmaṇas [are mentioned]—this is seen in the *Raurava* (according to the commentary on the *Mataṅgapārameśvara*, *Kriyāpāda* 5.93; it is not found in the printed edition of the *Raurava*, as noted in the marginal gloss on p. 113, note 6). It is heard [in scripture] that Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras are also included. Therefore, all four castes have the right (*adhikāra*) here. However, regarding the status of being a Guru:

Therefore, [the practice belongs] to the Brāhmaṇa alone, according to the Vedic revelation: "Then the excellent teacher, the illustrious one, the foremost-born, the most handsome" (Svāyambhuva-Āgama 15.1). || 99 ||
Not every Brāhmaṇa is a Guru;
rather—only one who, being authorized by the Guru, knows Śiva together with His powers, His presiding deities, and His manifestations, is a Guru worthy of honor. (100)
