The initiated one, having understood from the Saṃhitās that these powers of the Supreme Lord— beginning with Knowledge (jñāna)— [consist of] this entire range of principles, worlds, elements, and states of being, starting from Anāśrita down to the world of Kālāgnirudra; that this is what is to be presided over and what is to be accomplished, namely the enjoyment and liberation of bound souls (paśu)— thus [he understands] the Supreme Lord.
He knows that [reality] as determined by means of words, sentences, and logical proofs through the removal of erroneous cognition regarding its object;

he contemplates that very [reality] for the sake of accepting another self and for the application of ritual worship during initiation; such a person, established in knowledge, is [fit to be] a teacher by virtue of his status as a guru.

When appointed, the Guru is none other; as it has been said: "One who is ignorant, deluded, full of doubt, devoid of devotion, not knowing the reality, or who has not practiced the path of ritual action—such a person is not considered by us to be a Guru. (100)
Now, regarding those who have been initiated, should the Lord of All be known as having ascended into the intellect (*buddhi*), or as not having ascended into it?
In this regard:
"The manifestation of Śiva as being made manifest by the cognition of the intellect has been maintained by others."
By those who had not found the measurement of Śiva and were made to dwell among the sacrificial animals. || 101 ||

Objects are always perceived by the person only when they have ascended into the intellect (*buddhi*), not when they have not so ascended, for otherwise it would follow that the intellect and the other faculties are purposeless. Even the Supreme Lord is perceived as distinct from that [intellect];
thus, only an object that has ascended into the intellect is perceivable, and not otherwise in its isolated state. For instance: "Dharma and so forth [are known] through the grace of the Lord..."

For some, having abandoned the impurities of *rajas* and *tamas*, the intellect (*buddhi*) becomes a state of extremely pure *sattva*. In that state, some who are steeped in the Sāṃkhya view maintain that the Supreme Lord exists like a reflection and is thus the object of cognition by that [intellect] alone and not by anything else;
but that is not so, because it is inconclusive (*anaikāntikatvāt*). 101.
For instance:
"How can that [intellect], for which even the Self is not an object because it is the enjoyer rather than the object of enjoyment, manifest the self-luminous Lord Śaṅkara? (102)

For it is not the case that everything which is perceived is necessarily mounted upon the intellect (*buddhi*), because the self (*ātman*) is the enjoyer of the intellect; thus, since even that which is not mounted upon the intellect lacks the status of being perceived, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is unestablished. How then could the mounting upon the intellect of the Self-luminous Lord (*īśvara*), as will be described, be established? || 102 ||

But surely the Sāṃkhyas maintain that the *puruṣa* is perceived only as mounted upon the intellect (*buddhi*), for it is said—even for Kapila and Brahmā, the *puruṣa* is imperceptible; thus, experience consists in the merging of the reflections of both the subject and the object within the intellect, which stands in the place of a mirror. Consequently, everything is perceived only as determined by the intellect.
That too is incorrect—for this person, whose pride has arisen at all times, is not perceived;
there is no time in which he is not perceived by one who is present here. (103)
Even for a Buddhist, since a person does not perceive another person through a reflected image of that person, the postulation of such a reflection is entirely fruitless.
Furthermore:

"The relationship of prior and posterior is logical for the self and its cognition; [likewise] the state of being perceived and the perceiver. But this [relationship] is non-existent because that [self and cognition] do not exist. (104)

Because the self consists of a reflection, it would follow that it is an object and something to be enjoyed; and because the cognition of the intellect has that [self] as its object, it would follow that the intellect is the enjoyer. This must not be accepted by you, for this [position] is untenable—(see the second footnote on page 78 of the previous section)—[namely,] that "the person is also perceived because it is determined by the intellect. || 104 ||
Moreover:

If the person were subject to transformation, it would become an object of experience; if it were to enter the range of that [transformation], the intellect would become its opposite, and there would also be a contradiction in the philosophical system. (105)

In this way, because the self (*pums*) is an object of experience by virtue of being an object of the intellect (*buddhi*), it would—like the objects themselves—be subject to transformation; and because the intellect is the experiencer, its [supposed] permanence would be undermined. Thus, there is a contradiction with your own doctrine. Therefore, since the relationship between the experiencer and the experienced cannot otherwise be accounted for, the person (*puruṣa*) must indeed be that which has not ascended into the intellect.

It must be accepted as established through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*). How then [is this consistent] with what was previously stated in the section on experience (*bhoga-prakaraṇa*) in the *Bhoga-kārikā* (verse 60): "The person (*puruṣa*) is that which is to be illuminated by the awakening of the intellect (*buddhi*) regarding the manifest, the unmanifest, and the knower"?

It is not by way of being an object of illumination (*prakāśyatva*), but rather by way of being the agent (*kārakatva*); thus there is no contradiction. For it is in relation to the objects—the manifest and the unmanifest—that the awakening of the intellect occurs.

It has been stated that the Puruṣa, being utterly distinct because it is the illuminator of that [citta], shines by itself: "Then there is the abiding of the seer in its own nature" (Yoga Sūtra 1.3). || 105 ||

Let this be granted; however, since God is an object of knowledge, like the sun and other such things, He must be known only as mounted upon the intellect (*buddhi*). No, that is not so, because it is impossible. For instance:
"That modification of the internal organ which is called cognition [cannot reach] the Great Lord."
It is not capable of being manifested because it is a bond, like shackles and the like.

For since the nature of a *pāśa* (bond) consists in being an obstacle to the attainment of the highest good (*śreyas*), how could the intellect (*buddhi*) and the other faculties possess the quality of illuminating the supreme good whose essence is Śiva? Alternatively, if the intellect is a bond, it must be limited;

in that case, how could the reflection of the Supreme Lord—who is unlimited by space, time, and so forth—be possible within it, just as the reflection of the sun and such is not possible in a sword or similar objects?

However, the reflection of a single part of Him therein is nothing but an illusion, because, as we have stated elsewhere, the Blessed One has no parts due to His being partless: "When the intellect is limited, there can be no reflection of the Lord within it, because He is unlimited; just as [there is no reflection] of the sun in a sword, that which appears is merely an illusion regarding a portion of Him. (106)
Furthermore:
"The fetters possess the qualities of being combustible and suppressible; therefore, they do not belong to the Wielder of the Trident (Śiva).
They are desired for the illumination of the agent who performs the acts of burning and suppressing. (107)
Fire is not manifested as the agent of burning by means of the wood to be burned; nor is the sun, the illuminator, [manifested] by means of meteors which are themselves illuminated.

Wood and other such objects, which are combustible or suppressible by fire and the like—the agents of burning or suppression—are not seen to be illuminators [of that fire] by means of reflecting its image. And since the intellect is both an object of cognition and suppressible by the Blessed One, it cannot be the illuminator of Him. (107–108)

Is it not the case that there is an inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatā*) due to objects such as mirrors, which are combustible? To this we reply: there is no fault in that regard in your fundamental reasoning.
Furthermore, there is a contradiction with scripture (*āgama*) in this position. For instance, the author of the Sūtras [states]: "By means of the pure reality of the self, known as consciousness..."
Speaking thus: "Śiva is to be meditated upon when the portions of Śiva and Śakti are purified. (109)
The author of the *Raurava-sūtra* declared to us that Maheśāna is unattainable by means of bonds (*pāśa*).

He stated that Śiva is to be meditated upon through the power of knowledge alone—that is, by the stainless power of Śiva which has been kindled. He further said that the Blessed Lord is not to be meditated upon by means of the intellect (*buddhi*), for [the Lord] is situated therein, absorbed, and the ointment of all.

In that [system], the sequence of the lines is seen as follows: "The *ātmatattva* (principle of self), free from all impurities (*añjana*), arisen from the *kalā* of Śiva and Śakti—this pure *ātmatattva* is proclaimed for practitioners. Then, the wise one, established therein, should contemplate that *kalā* through absorption into his own essential nature" (Raurava Sūtrasaṃgraha 4.42–43). || 109 ||
Thus, in this way—the Lord is neither an object of meditation nor an object of knowledge for those bound by the subtle fetters. (110)
Therefore, Śiva cannot be known by means of the intellect and other faculties, nor can He be meditated upon by those initiated solely through their exclusive focus on them. || 110 ||

How, then, is Śiva known? It is said: "The Self, its veils removed, perceives Śiva along with Śakti and the other [principles] by means of the vision of consciousness empowered by the rays of the power of the Śiva-sun. (111)

Just as the world perceives the sun by means of an eye aided by the sun, so too is the Supreme Lord perceived by those devotees devoted to the knowledge of reality who are graced by Him—by the very power of knowledge whose veils have been removed and whose capacity has been augmented through the grace of the Supreme Lord. Is He seen as an object, like a jar or other such things? No.
No, because since both the seer and the seen are all-pervasive, such a perception is impossible. || 111 ||
Thus,

since the knowledge of Śiva is seen even in an atom endowed with all [impurities] through the practice of the means of yoga based on the word "Śiva" when [the soul] has reached Śiva who is beyond bonds, how could that [knowledge] come about? (112)
If [the scripture] is inaccessible due to the fetters (pāśa), how can there be comprehension from it for those whose souls are initiated?
Since sound is a fetter by virtue of being the cause of space and air, how can there be comprehension of that [reality] from it? || 112 ||
To this it is replied:
Śiva is manifest in the word consisting of mantra and tantra, as well as in the kalās;
the eye of consciousness (ciccakṣus) confirms this, and therefore nothing is contradictory. || 113 ||

Because the Blessed One is always and everywhere present through his presiding presence, he is indeed accompanied by all [deities] at all times; however, he is said to be "manifest" when there is a special proximity due to his acting as a bestower of grace in a particular *liṅga*, *maṇḍala*, or in the presence of the *ācārya* and others.
For this very reason, acts such as worship and prostration performed there become the cause of fruits for the performers, whereas they do not elsewhere. It is just like that.
Even in the gross form of the *pāśa* (the bond), namely the words of mantra and tantra, as well as in their constituent parts such as *nāda*, *bindu*, and so forth,

the Lord manifests consciousness and reveals His own Self to men; thus, this expressive power of mantras is unprecedented compared to that of words denoting jars and the like— this has been stated by us in the *Mantravārttika-ṭīkā*.

For instance: Śiva is manifest within the subtle bonds because he is distinct from the effects of bondage; this is known through his manifest effect, just as the presence of the individual soul is known in the body through its manifest activity. (114)

Just as the body of certain humans is known to be presided over by a deity because its instructions regarding matters of the three times are unfailing, so too, from the utterance of mantra-sounds and the arrangement of their written syllables,
one observes effects such as subjugation (*vaśya*) that are distinct from what could arise from mere sound; therefore, the Blessed One is manifested therein.
It is understood as being like [the perception of a deity] in a statue and so forth. || 114 ||
In this regard:
"Among all these latent dispositions (anu-bandha), existence (bhava) manifests itself and others;
how can it be said to be manifested within those things that are devoid of manifestation? (115)
The meaning is that the manifestation of the nature of consciousness (cidrūpa) in an insentient object (jaḍa) is not logically tenable. || 115 ||
This is not a fault:

just as a lamp is manifested as the burner of its fuel and so forth when there is something to be burned, so too this [consciousness] of those possessing intellect is the illuminator of both itself and others when [objects] are themselves non-luminous. (116)

Since the lamp serves as an illustration, just as the Self— which, though insentient in the bodies of humans and others, is all-pervasive and illuminates both itself and others— manifests in accordance with karma for the benefit of these sentient beings such as humans,
so too does the Supreme Lord manifest within images, paintings, and the sounds of mantras for the sake of assisting bound souls (paśus).
There is no fault, for [the universal] is manifested through the proximity of a particular (viśeṣa). || 116 ||

Thus, for those who have been initiated, there is the destruction of this bond through knowledge. When does one attain equality with Śiva? It is said: "The teacher and the initiated both attain equality with Śiva.
Through initiation, only those karmas whose effects have not yet begun are destroyed, not those whose effects have already commenced.

As it is heard: "The initiated enter that supreme peace upon the dissolution of the body. For them, however, this dissolution occurs through initiation alone (*sadyonirvāṇadīkṣā*), not through [the exhaustion of] experience.
In that very same way, at the end of the yoga, the practitioner will certainly attain accomplishment.

As it is heard: "Having enjoyed pleasures for a very long time, accompanied by hosts of celestial nymphs, their longing subsided, they become partakers of the supreme sovereignty of the state of Śiva. || 117 ||

It has been stated that liberation, along with its means, has been explained. Now, however, in determining this [matter], there is the refutation of supreme liberation [as held by others]. Regarding this, Mahāvratas says: "If the Siddhas were equal to Śiva, there would be a multiplicity of causes."
Because their intellects are unequal, an effect cannot arise from them. || 118 ||

Even for the liberated ones, if they possessed universal agency like the Lord, there would be the undesirable consequence that no effects could ever arise, because they would hold conflicting opinions such as "let this be new" or "let this be old. Therefore, it must be accepted that the liberated possess only omniscience, while universal agency belongs solely to the Supreme Lord. || 118 ||
This is not a fault:
"Because of being possessed by passion, hatred, and so forth, men possess unequal knowledge;
because their intellects are unequal, a diversity of desires is not difficult to find. (119)
It is indeed logical that among animals there is a divergence of intention due to their attachment to particular sides through the influence of passion and other defects;

however, the Siddhas—being free from the faults of passion and the like, and possessing an intellect whose range encompasses all objects—are therefore not possessed of those conflicting desires. (120)
Those [powers] have been declared by Śiva and by the wise to have undivided authority;
therefore, the production of all effects here is not contradicted.

Since they, by virtue of being perfected (*siddha*), are free from passion and the like, are knowers of all objects as they truly are, possess an office inseparable from Śiva, and are all-powerful creators, it is impossible for them to take sides; thus, there is no difference of intention among them, and consequently, the fault of the non-production of the effect does not arise here. || 121 ||
In the Mahāvratapakṣa, however, liberation itself is denied, because: "It is incorrect to say that one who is not an omniscient agent is liberated;
for due to deficiency he lacks omniscience, and due to his lack of agency he is like a bound soul (paśu). (122)

For liberation is indeed supreme perfection; yet a state of non-omniscience has been attained. Due to the absence of the power to act as the creator of all, the liberated one would become like a beast. || 122 ||
Through the manifestation of consciousness, the perfected ones (siddhas) possess universal agency, just like Īśvara;
otherwise, they would have no agency at all, just as Īśvara would not [if he lacked it]. (123)

Through the manifestation of consciousness (*cidvyakti*), the state of being the agent of all indeed exists. Just as the state of being the agent of all is established for the perfected ones (*siddhas*), so too does the Lord (*īśvara*) possess the agency over all things due to his omniscience; otherwise, this universal agency would not exist, leading to the undesirable consequence that the universe would never arise. || 123 ||
Moreover—
the manifestation of the power of agency is not logically possible upon the destruction of consciousness;
for it has been stated previously that this power is one alone, namely knowledge and action (jñāna-kriyā), and there is no manifestation of it through the aspect of consciousness.

Non-manifestation is logically consistent with the aspect of action (kriyāṃśa), because that aspect is partless (niraṃśatva). Nor is there a deviation [from this rule] in the case of the manifestations of the powers of the Vidyās and Īśvaras, since those powers never exist in a state of manifestation.

Now, if it is argued that, like the Sāṃkhya, the agency of persons does not exist even previously, that too is incorrect—because the non-existence of agency has [already] been refuted, since that [agency] was established. (124)

Devoid of all cognitive and active powers, partless, and solitary, he is a bound soul (*paśu*). Since agency was previously established in the section on experience (*bhoga-prakaraṇa*), when that [agency] is unmanifest, the power of knowledge is likewise unmanifest due to its identity with it; thus, by the deficiency of all cognitive and active powers, he is indeed a bound soul.
"He would be liberated. || 124 ||
Furthermore, in this regard, the opponent [objects]:
"Agency is manifested [only] when [the self] is established, and it is not like cognition, which exists everywhere. (125)
Thinking, "There exists a Lord who is the creator of all," one performs what is to be done.

However, the agency that belongs to a Siddha is not like that of a knower; for a Siddha does not perform what is to be done after reflecting, "Since I am the creator of everything everywhere, what more remains for me to do? (125)
If this is so, then if [the soul] is established as manifest in the bound soul (paśu), what distinction is there between those two? || 126 ||
One who has attained perfection would not perform any actions, for the state of being the agent of all things belongs to the perfected one.
If the agency of the perfected one, even when manifest, does not produce an effect, then what distinction is there between him and the bound soul (paśu), whose agency is unmanifest? || 126 ||
For instance:
"Activity (pravṛtti) exists in the production of all things; manifestation (vyakti), however, is nothing other than that which belongs to them. (127)
Knowledge that has proceeded toward the illumination of all things is called "manifest" (vyakta).
This very manifestation of its agency is what distinguishes it from a bound soul (paśu), namely, that its engagement with everything is like that of knowledge itself.
Thus, in this way, it should be described that [the Lord] does not exist even when engaged in all activities. || 128 ||
Either the cessation of vision (*dṛṅnirodha*) or a defect existing prior to liberation must be accepted.

If the manifest power of action (*kriyāśakti*) of the perfected being (*siddha*) is evident, it must be admitted as capable of all effects. If, however, even when manifest, it does not produce an effect, then—just like the power of an atom containing a reflection—it simply does not exist for him at all.

This must be stated. Now, if it is said that [the power] exists unmanifested (*avyakta*), then, because the powers of knowledge and action are one, liberation must be defined as the cessation of vision (*dṛk-nirodha*) or the non-manifestation of knowledge. Or, if it is maintained that even by means of that unmanifested [power], the power of knowledge is manifested, then in the case of that Supreme Śiva for whom liberation was previously non-existent— [The text continues: ...in Him... [the following objection is raised]. If it is argued that the power of knowledge is not manifested by that [unmanifested power], then there would be no manifestation of the power of knowledge at all; consequently, since the power of action is also dependent upon the power of knowledge, there would be no manifestation of the power of action either. Thus, the entire universe would remain eternally unmanifested. Furthermore, if it is argued that the power of knowledge is manifested by that [unmanifested power], then, because the power of action is likewise dependent upon the power of knowledge, the power of action too would be manifested by that very same [unmanifested power]. Consequently, since both powers would be manifested simultaneously, the cessation of vision (*dṛk-nirodha*) would not exist, and thus liberation would be impossible. Therefore, this [position] is untenable. Alternatively, if it is argued that the power of knowledge is manifested by that [unmanifested power] while the power of action is not, then the power of action would never be manifested, and thus the universe would remain eternally unmanifested. Since the defect of non-agency has been stated [to apply] to the omniscient one as it does to the liberated, you must accept one from among these four positions. And since there is no defect whatsoever in the first position here, liberation must be accepted as being equal to Śiva, characterized precisely by omniscience and omnipotence. 118.

The Pāśupatas, however, claim that upon liberation, through the transference of the qualities of Īśvara, the perfected ones (siddhas) attain equality with Śiva; that is incorrect—for if there were a transference of qualities at the time of liberation, Īśvara would become non-Īśvara. (129)
Upon the transfer of a portion of a quality, that quality would become possessed of parts.

Indeed, if the transfer of the qualities of God were admitted, God himself would become devoid of qualities such as omniscience; for since qualities are partless, it is impossible for them to be transferred in part.
Furthermore:
Qualities do not leave their own possessor to go to another possessor. (130)

Furthermore, this established order of entities is contradicted if it is maintained that qualities reside in another quality-substance by abandoning their own quality-substance; for in that case, everything would possess all qualities,
which would result in the impossibility of the observed rule and entail the absurd consequence that one who is liberated would be both liberated and unliberated.
Since the transference of qualities is logically untenable, one must not accept equality with Śiva on that basis. || 130 ||

However, those who know the Vedānta maintain that liberation consists in attaining equality with Him through absorption into Him; yet that too is incorrect, because the Supreme Self is just like the individual self which was previously shown to be afflicted by defects. (131)

Since the Siddha has attained absorption into that [Supreme Self] and is non-different from it, the defect of insentience and so forth—which was previously established as belonging to the Supreme Self because of its being the material cause—would necessarily apply to the Siddha as well due to his non-difference from it; thus, for you, liberation is nothing other than non-duality (advaita). || 131 ||
Moreover:
The view of oneness is the means to liberation, yet it is sublated by one's own self. (132)

Since that [liberation] cannot exist if there is no distinction between those who are to be liberated and those who effect their liberation, it follows that Brahman alone is real—“one only, without a second. Therefore, the claim that knowledge of That alone is the means to liberation is contradicted by one’s own statement, like saying "my mother is barren. For if there is oneness, [the distinction between the two does not exist].
There is the relationship of the probandum and the probans; or, in the case of the relationship of the probandum and the probans, there is multiplicity. || 132 ||
Furthermore:
"The operation of the means of valid cognition is held to occur only when there is difference, and not otherwise. (133)
Why do the learned not accept this non-difference as established?

For if that very means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) by which your "Brahman alone is real" is established were itself unreal—like something seen in a dream—how could the establishment of the real Brahman proceed from it? But if it is real, then [the conclusion follows].

Since the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), the knower (*pramātṛ*), the object of knowledge (*prameya*), and the resulting cognition (*pramiti*) are all real, how could non-duality (*advaita*) be unreal? Therefore, how can its attainment also be liberation (*mokṣa*)?
As for the Sāṃkhyas, they say:
"Having abandoned the delightful fruit of yoga as well as the worldly enjoyments," [they seek liberation]. (133–134)
And how could others have declared that liberation (mokṣa) is isolation (kaivalya), which is insentience?

Yoga is the body of Sadāśiva; having abandoned that characteristic fruit—which is liberation consisting of omniscience and so forth—and having also abandoned the enjoyments of saṃsāra, which are the fruits of various perceptions of sense-objects and are accomplished through powers such as *aṇimā*.

Out of a desire for isolation (*kaivalya*), they have imagined that liberation consists merely in the knowledge of their own selves as being dissociated from *prakṛti*, which is equivalent to the destruction of the self.
Furthermore, no one can be motivated toward such a state, as it does not constitute a human goal (*puruṣārtha*). || 134 ||
For thus:
how could those who are virtuous ever act for the destruction of their own consciousness? (135)

Who indeed are those wise ones who would daily exert effort in the practice of discernment and insight for the sake of destroying the knowledge of their own Self? (135) Who, being learned, would daily undertake the labor of practicing the yoga of knowledge and so forth to destroy the very knowledge of their own Self? (135)
Furthermore:
"Discrimination (viveka) is indeed [the knowledge] of the difference between the qualities (guṇas) and the Puruṣa by way of their distinct properties. (136)
In that regard, whatever [is claimed to be] "vision" is not tenable upon investigation;
furthermore, when investigation is conducted, the Sāṃkhya theory of knowledge having the qualities (guṇas) and the person (puruṣa) as its object is not tenable.
For instance, do the *guṇas* themselves demonstrate their distinction from the *puruṣa*, or does the *puruṣa* perceive it by himself? In this regard:
"The *guṇas* are indeed characterized by the qualities of being agents and producing [effects]. (137)
They demonstrate to the person that "you" are not [the agent], showing him the objects situated within the intellect (*buddhi*).

For it is accepted that the Person (*puruṣa*) perceives objects only as they are presented by the intellect, since the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*) is unchanging, non-transitive, has its objects revealed [by another], pure, and infinite; thus, we [perceive] only through the qualities (*guṇa*) mounted upon the intellect.
Those [entities] are endowed with attributes such as agency and are mutually intermingled; however, you are not so—thus his discrimination must be demonstrated.
What follows from this? And therefore:
"If one perceives them as they have been thus shown, the person becomes a perceiver of falsehood. (138)

It is utterly untenable that liberation could be accomplished through false vision (*mithyādarśana*). For if the Puruṣa were to perceive the qualities as they are presented by the intellect (*buddhi*), it would be impossible for the intellect to have unlimited qualities as its object, since the intellect is itself limited. As it has been said: "Even for Kapila and Brahmā, the qualities are not directly perceived."

Thus, they must be subsumed under the Buddha by way of a partial aspect. The non-comprehension of reality through a partial aspect is [as follows]: the comprehension of the Himavat mountain as "Blue Mountain" with respect to the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of blueness is indeed false. And liberation does not arise from false knowledge, because that would be illogical. || 138 ||
For these qualities, such as agency and the like, are indeed qualities; [the realization] "I am not these" is of such a nature. (139)
In the case of perception being attributed to the Puruṣa, the state of "that which has been shown being perceived" is destroyed.

What you have stated—that an object is perceived by the Puruṣa only when it is presented by the intellect—is contradicted if one assumes that the Puruṣa directly perceives the guṇas as distinct from its own self. || 139 ||

Now it is said: the Puruṣa does not perceive the Guṇas directly, nor do they show themselves to him by ascending into the intellect (buddhi), because that would contradict what has been stated. Rather, they merely show the difference between the Guṇas and the Puruṣa.
That also is not so, because:
They do not show that "the qualities are one thing and the person is another. (140)
O treasury of wisdom, since the qualities are not distinct from the possessor of qualities, they cannot be their objects;
thus it was declared previously that [the self] is atomic.

For if they do not reveal their own nature, then it follows that they must reveal the distinctness of other qualities. Yet, there can be no qualities other than those characterized as the repository of cognition—that is, the storehouse of intellect—within the treasury of consciousness. Furthermore, it has been stated previously that their self is not their object: "If the person were subject to transformation, he would become an object of experience, and [the qualities] would fall within his range."
(Śloka 105) Thus, how could they demonstrate that [the object] is other than that when it is not their domain? (140–141)
Therefore, a vision whose object is discrimination is not possible.

Since the vision of discrimination is thus untenable, how can there be the attainment of isolation (*kaivalya*), which is liberation? Consequently, you must accept that liberation consists of omniscience and other such qualities.
What can be said of the Śākta and other views? It is said: because of the absence of both the goal and the means within the aforementioned bonds of the bound souls (paśu-pāśa). (142)
Therefore, the views of the disputants, which consist of fetters, should be abandoned by the wise.

For, since the objects of the bound soul and the objects of the fetters have been established through valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa) as described, that which is to be accomplished—namely liberation—and the vision of its cessation are the means; yet [those disputants] do not establish these, because they are beyond their scope.
Therefore, those who seek the highest good must avoid the views of other proponents, for they yield results that are not conducive to well-being. || 142 ||
And for this very reason: it reveals the specific distinctions of the bound soul (paśu), the fetters (pāśa), and so forth, without contradiction. (143)
Since it possesses that superior meaning, for what wise person would the Śaiva system not be dear?

For it is not the case that the categories of *paśu* (the bound soul), *pāśa* (the bond), and so forth are unseen by other philosophical systems; rather, they are seen as they truly are, yet in their specific distinctions (*vaiśiṣṭya*).
Thus, it reveals those distinctions. Therefore, as previously stated, it apprehends what has not been apprehended by perception and inference.
To whom is the well-proclaimed authority known as the Śaiva Āgama not acceptable, just like perception and other means of valid cognition? || 143 ||

If it is argued that this [Tantra] cannot be authoritative because other traditions (anvāgama) are also authoritative and thus contradict it, it is replied here: even though it proceeds in opposition to the view of the *pāśas*, it does not lose its status as a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇatā*),
because in this system, all *pāśas* are to be severed from every side.

By this [subsequent cognition], other views are not set aside; rather, because it arises precisely as a sublater of that object which consists of a snare—namely, by means of the view "this is not so"—it is unable to invalidate its own validity due to that contradiction, just as in the case of the cognition "this is not silver, but merely mother-of-pearl. Nor is there any contradiction between this and other views, since:
And yet, within their own respective domains, these do not invalidate their status as valid cognitions.

Furthermore, that authority known as Śaiva does not establish the unreality of other perspectives, such that there would be a contradiction between it and them; rather, just like perception and the other means of knowledge, its status as a valid authority consists precisely in its capacity to lead one to what is to be attained, even though it reveals only a limited portion of reality. This has been stated by us in the *Sarvāgamaprāmāṇya*. 145.
Moreover—
[it is] as they say regarding those [scriptures], which permit the conduct of the castes and stages of life (*varṇāśramācāra*):
(see the third footnote on page 129 of the previous section).

"One should not transgress the conduct of the castes and stages of life even in thought. "Whoever, while remaining in a particular stage of life, is initiated into the teaching of Śiva, should remain steadfast in that very stage and protect the Dharma of Śiva. For this very reason, even from your own perspective, he does not possess the status of a heretic (*pāṣaṇḍa*), because there is no contradiction with the Vedas. Furthermore, it is heard in scripture that he is accepted by those who know the Vedas.

In the Purāṇas, Itihāsas, and other texts, there is recorded the performance of this [rite] by great sages such as Śveta and Upamanyu, and in the Mahābhārata by Nara-Nārāyaṇa and Aśvatthāman. From these instances, it is known that "the Lord was worshipped by you in a Liṅga, and in every age in an image. Furthermore, in the Suvarṇākṣa episode, success was attained through the worship of the Supreme Lord by Kṛṣṇa, who is the most beloved in the world. Moreover, there is another [instance]. Kṛṣṇa is the dearest in the world.
"It shall come to pass; and the entire world shall exist within your mouth, of this there is no doubt"—thus it is stated in the *Rāmāyaṇa*.

In the *Smṛtis* regarding Kārtavīrya and others, dharma is preceded by the establishment [of shrines], as in: "He who properly constructs a temple of Śiva built of baked bricks... and in the *Sūtra*: "Therein, one should point out liberation. And such things are observed.
Pṛthukeśvara, Rāmeśvara, and others have been consecrated.

Furthermore, in the Vedas—specifically in the Śvetāśvatara and other branches as well as in the Atharvaśiras and other mantras—there is a clear recognition of Śiva. Consequently, there is no contradiction, nor is there a lack of foundational authority, nor is it accepted by only a few, such that [the objection would apply].
Even from your perspective, there would be a lack of authoritative validity.
Furthermore:
Nor is its object obstructed by any other means of valid cognition. (146)
Therefore, even those learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*) should accept this as a means that yields results superior to [other] fruits;
nor has it been stated previously in the section on experience (*bhoga-prakaraṇa*) that this is sublated by either perception or inference—
which would render it invalid like the injunction "one should sprinkle with fire"— and thus everything is consistent.
This [scripture], which is the cause of the supreme good, should be accepted as authoritative by those who know the Veda and by others as well. || 146 ||
Nor is this [view] sublated by other views, because:
"It is not sublated by those [views], nor by these, nor by general [views]. (147)

Because it is distinct from those [Vedas] and because they do not constitute its object, the composition of the Vedas and other such works does not deviate from having an author. Hiraṇyagarbha and others are remembered by the learned as their authors. And in the Gītā: "I am the author of the Vedānta and the knower of the Veda" (15.15).

Furthermore, because they teach doctrines whose meanings are mutually contradictory, they are not omniscient. As it has been said: "If Sugata is omniscient, what proof is there that Kapila is not? Or if both are omniscient, how can there be a difference in their opinions?
[This refers to the general authorship by those who are not omniscient.]

Even those views have non-universal objects and are sublated by the treatises composed by the Omniscient One; how then could that very [Omniscient One]—who, being the author of those [treatises], is as will be explained, distinct from them by virtue of determining the meaning of all other scriptures and having made that [reality] his object—be sublated by them? For it is not the case that he is apprehended by them in the same manner that they are apprehended by him.
Just as in the case of the fruit of the object of cognition, they appear by following after that [object]. || 148 ||
The distinction [of the means of knowledge] as being established upon its own object and result has not been made in that way;
rather, having stated its object and result, it is shown to be dependent upon its own object and result. (149)
Therefore, that distinctness does not fall within the range of those [limited] perceptions;

for just as that Shaiva reality exists, so too the distinctness regarding the object and fruit of those views is mounted upon their own respective objects and fruits. The Buddhists are established in the principle of cognition (*buddhitattva*), while the Jains are established in the qualities (*guṇa*).

Having restated [the opponent's position] with "ityādi" and so forth, [it is argued that] [the cognition] shines forth as having all things as its object; however, the object of its result cannot be made an objective domain by all of those [cognitions] in such a way. Therefore, how could they possess sublativeness (*bādhakatva*) with respect to that which is not their own object? || 149 ||
For this very reason: "Therefore, permission or prohibition is definitively established in relation to those [actions]. (150)
The perception of those [scriptures] belonging to the same class is pervaded by [the fact that they] are not the object of Śiva’s knowledge;

since they are weak due to being composed by non-omniscient beings, there is only acceptance of their practice regarding their own specific objects insofar as they do not contradict the Śaiva Āgamas. (This refers to the third footnote on page 129 of the preceding work.)

[She] should be regarded [in this way]. One should not transgress the conduct of the castes and stages of life even in thought; however, in case of conflict with that, one should perform the prohibition, or else one should perform the Brāhmī [initiation], or indeed the Śaivī initiation by necessity. || 150 ||

However, an object within the scope of Śaiva knowledge is never pervaded by that [knowledge] which possesses the same origin as those [scriptures] composed by non-omniscient beings. Nor does it follow that this [Śaiva knowledge] is impermanent because it is an effect; for:
"Even though it possesses those qualities, it has been established in the Śaiva [tradition] from beginningless time. (151)

And that which correctly discerns [reality] is said to be the Śaiva knowledge (*jñāna*). For scripture (*āgama*) consists of both word and meaning. In this regard, although the form of the *tantra* is created by Īśvara, it possesses eternality because its meaning—the quality of perfect knowledge and so forth—is inherent in the Supreme Lord and is eternal. For this very reason, it is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
For this very reason:
"And because his power remains unimpeded, the Lord does not suffer sublation by that [limited cognition]. (152)
Therefore, it does not even have an equal result; how then could it be fruitless?
It is neither fruitless, nor does it have a result equal to other views, nor is its result sublated;
rather, its validity has already been stated, because the Blessed One, possessing unimpeded power, is supreme over all. || 152 ||
Or even if there were equality with other systems of vision, nevertheless, initiation is not an optional means, because:
"Even though the result is equal, liberation is attained through initiation alone. (153)

Since it grants success to men through a very brief practice, who indeed would abandon a means for achieving their desired goal that is so much easier and instead engage in something extremely extensive that causes only suffering? As it has been said: "If one can find honey right here, why should one go to the mountain? When the desired object is attained, who..."
Knowing this, one should exert effort. Thus [ends the verse]. 153.
Moreover:
Accomplishment is free from activity, and liberation is even more transcendent.
Who would not embrace that means of proof adorned with the authority of the Vedas?
Since it is heard that the fruit of this scripture is the most excellent of all, who would not engage in it while setting aside others?
Thus, although the results are equal according to other perspectives, there is no optionality regarding engagement here. || 154 ||
But how is it said that this was composed by the Supreme Lord? To this it is replied:
"Liberation and worldly enjoyment, along with their means, which have descended through a lineage from Śiva, were fully revealed to Ātreya by Ruru, the lord of sages. (155)
Sadyojyotis, his mind permeated with compassion, has clearly and concisely composed these two [works] for the sake of awakening those of dull intellect. (156)
And that which the Blessed One, who is honored as the Lord, the illustrious teacher Ugrajyotis—the ocean of all branches of knowledge—instructed; 157.
Thus ends the *Mokṣakārikā*.

It is understood that this very uninterrupted continuity of remembrance, received through the lineage of the Guru, is the cause of all supreme welfare by virtue of its being the nature of the Supreme Lord. || 155–157 ||
Thus, this commentary on the *Mokṣakārikā*, composed for the benefit of disciples in brief by Bhaṭṭa Rāmakaṇṭha, the son of Nārāyaṇakaṇṭha, has been completed.
Thus ends the commentary on the *Mokṣakārikā* composed by Bhaṭṭa Rāmakaṇṭha, son of the illustrious Nārāyaṇakaṇṭha.
